activities.title: Your First Optimization Model
activities.description: The Sawyer Furniture Co. makes tables and chairs. Tables profit $120, chairs $80. A table needs 4 hours of carpentry and 2 of finishing; a chair needs 3 and 1. This week: 240 carpentry hours, 100 finishing hours. What should they build?

steps.title: Guess first
steps.description: Write down your intuitive production plan and its profit. Keep it — we check it against the optimum at the end.

steps.title: Name the three ingredients
steps.description: Decision variables (tables T, chairs C), objective (maximize 120T + 80C), constraints (4T + 3C ≤ 240, 2T + C ≤ 100, T, C ≥ 0).

steps.title: Solve it in Colab
steps.description: Run the gurobipy cell and read the optimal plan and profit. Compare with your guess — the room's best guess usually leaves 10-20% on the table.

steps.title: Break it
steps.description: Chair profit rises to $110. Carpentry loses 40 hours. Re-solve after each change and watch the decision — not just the profit — flip.

codeBlock.code:
import gurobipy as gp
from gurobipy import GRB

m = gp.Model('sawyer_furniture')
T = m.addVar(name='tables')
C = m.addVar(name='chairs')

m.setObjective(120*T + 80*C, GRB.MAXIMIZE)
m.addConstr(4*T + 3*C <= 240, 'carpentry_hours')
m.addConstr(2*T + 1*C <= 100, 'finishing_hours')

m.optimize()
print(f'Build {T.X:.0f} tables and {C.X:.0f} chairs')
print(f'Max weekly profit: ${m.ObjVal:,.0f}')

activities.discussionNote: Notice what the solver gives you that a spreadsheet cannot: a certificate of optimality. It is not a good answer — it is provably the best answer. That guarantee is what companies pay for.

takeaways.text: Prescriptive analytics is the top of the value chain: descriptive → predictive → prescriptive. Prediction is an input; the decision is the product.
Every optimization model — from tonight's furniture problem to Microsoft's cloud — has exactly three ingredients: decision variables, an objective, and constraints.
Solvers don't just find good answers; they find provably optimal ones — and the gap between intuition and optimal is where careers and Edelman Awards are made.
